newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-EMI unveils blueprint for monetary rigour.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-EMI unveils blueprint for monetary rigour.

text.p: Europe's Monetary Institute on Friday unveiled its blueprint for a fiercely anti-inflationary European central bank of the future that will ensure the planned single currency is every bit as stable as the German mark.

In a long-awaited report, the EMI presented a comprehensive monetary policy toolkit for the new central bank, endowing it with the policy strengths of the powerful German Bundesbank, which already dictates the level of interest rates in Europe.
The European Central Bank, like the Bundesbank, will have price stability as its ultimate goal when it takes over responsibility for monetary policy once the single currency is launched in 1999.

Under the EMI's game plan for its successor -- which has to be approved by the ECB next year -- the new bank will conduct policy mainly through open market operations, with two further interest rates setting upper and lower limits for short-term rates.

Its main open market tool -- a two-week 'reverse transaction' is a mirror of the Bundesbank's securities repurchase tenders. The upper limit on money market rates will also be very close to the Bundesbank's Lombard facility.

EMI chief Alexandre Lamfalussy, mindful that many smaller European countries are nervous of being trampled over by Europe's largest economy, went out of his way to stress that this was not simply a copy of the German central bank.

"There is an idea that the European central bank copies the operating framework of the Bundesbank, but it does not," the EMI president told a news conference in Frankfurt. "We have not taken over any model from any one country."

German Finance Minister Theo Waigel welcomed the blueprint as paving the way for price stability in the euro zone. "Price stability and solid finances are the indispensible pillars of a successful currency union," he said in a statement.
Although it gave very precise details in some areas, the EMI report left several key decisions up to the ECB itself after it is set up in the middle of next year.
It left open the decision of exactly what form of policy strategy the ECB will adopt, simply recommending that it target either inflation or the money supply.

It said it had considered five possible monetary strategies that the ECB could adopt, and had eliminated the possibility of exchange rate targeting, interest rate pegging or nominal income targeting as they did not meet overall requirements.

"Taking into account a number of guiding principles...and considering the environment likely to prevail in the euro area, the list of potential candidate strategies has been narrowed down to two, namely monetary targeting and direct inflation targeting," the EMI said.
It also left open the question of whether the European Central Bank would use minimum reserves -- which require banks to deposit some funds at the central bank -- in its policy.
The Bundesbank has pushed hard for the inclusion of this instrument but others, such as Britain, reject the idea.

The EMI also sat on the fence on an issue close to the City of London's heart -- the question of whether banks in non-euro European countries will be given full access to the TARGET payments transfers system.
London fears that exclusion from some parts of this will hurt its banking industry if Britain decides to stay out of the euro.

Analysts generally welcomed the plans, saying they created the basis for sound monetary policy. But they warned that it was essential that the central bank remains independent of politicians if its policies were to prove effective.

"The Bundesbank did not build its reputation on the fact that it had a Lombard rate or minimum reserves -- but on the fact that it was able to withstand political pressure for a looser monetary policy," said Joachim Fels at Morgan Stanley.
"The key question is -- will the ECB be able to fend off political pressure for lower interest rates?" he added.
